html:
The Yassa was the law of the Mongol Empire, a body of decrees said to have been laid down by Genghis Khan and built up during his reign from 1206. It was kept secret and never published, so no full text survives.

It seems to have grown out of wartime orders, which were later written down and extended to cover daily life and custom. Genghis Khan's adopted son Shigi Qutuqu, the chief judge, kept the records, and his second son Chagatai was put in charge of enforcing it. Chagatai had a reputation for strictness.

What we know of its contents comes from outside writers, such as the Persian historian Juvayni, and is patchy. Rules that are often mentioned include:

  • harsh punishments, often death, for theft, desertion and disobedience in war
  • rules on hunting, the army and the sharing of loot
  • respect for envoys, whose killing was a cause for war
  • freedom for all religions and tax exemptions for clergy

Because it was secret, rulers could use it as they liked. Historians still argue whether a single written code ever existed or whether "the Yassa" was a name for the khan's accumulated rulings and Mongol custom.

Its prestige outlived the empire. Later Mongol and Turkic rulers, including Timur and the Mughals, claimed to honour it. In 1640 the western Mongols wrote a new law, the Mongol and Oirat Code, for a Buddhist steppe.
sum: The Yassa was the law of the Mongol Empire, a body of decrees said to have been laid down by Genghis Khan and built up during his reign from 1206. It was kept secret and never published, so no full text survives.
